const std::string VALID_GRADES = "ABCDF";

}

The key formal rule is this: the compiler internally rewrites the range-based for loop as a traditional iterator loop, calling `begin()` and `end()` on the range. For a raw C-style `char` array, the compiler knows its size at compile time and can generate those bounds automatically.

The critical distinction from a traditional `for` loop is that you never manage an index variable — you declare what **type** you want to receive on each iteration, and the compiler handles the traversal.

The formal term for what you have described is a **dangling reference**. The C++ standard is explicit on this: when a lambda captures a local variable by reference, the lambda does not extend the lifetime of that variable in any way. If the variable is destroyed — because it goes out of scope, or because the owning object is deallocated — the lambda is left holding a reference to memory that is no longer valid. Any subsequent access through that reference is **undefined behavior**. [1](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/lambda)

In the context of `cv.wait()`, this is especially dangerous because the wait may outlive the stack frame where `ready` was declared. This is actually one of the motivating reasons why `std::unique_ptr` and shared ownership patterns (covered in your Week 6 material) exist: to give the programmer precise, explicit control over object lifetimes rather than relying on stack scope alone.
